q.t: The shine of a polished metal is called…
q.e: Lustre is the shine of metals when polished (metallic lustre).

q.t: A metal that can be beaten into thin sheets is…
q.e: Malleable means it can be hammered flat. Aluminium foil is an example.

q.t: A metal that can be drawn into wires is…
q.e: Ductile means it can be stretched into wires, like copper wire.

q.t: A school bell rings when struck. This property is called…
q.e: Sonorous metals make a ringing sound when struck.

q.t: Which metal is a liquid at room temperature?
q.e: Mercury is the metal that is liquid at room temperature, which is why it was used in thermometers.

q.t: Which two things are both needed for iron to rust?
q.e: The three-bottle experiment shows rust forms only when both air (oxygen) and water are present.

q.t: Coating iron with zinc to stop rusting is called…
q.e: Galvanisation puts a zinc layer on iron, keeping air and water away from it.

q.t: Sodium is stored in…
q.e: Sodium reacts strongly with air and water. Kerosene keeps both away.

q.t: Phosphorus is stored in…
q.e: Phosphorus catches fire in air, so it is kept under water.

q.t: Non-metals like coal and sulfur break when hammered. They are…
q.e: Brittle substances break into pieces instead of flattening.

q.t: Which are the most malleable metals?
q.e: Gold and silver can be beaten into extremely thin sheets — silver foil on sweets is one example.

q.t: Which metals are soft enough to cut with a knife?
q.e: Sodium and potassium are exceptions — metals that are very soft.

q.t: Which non-metal conducts electricity?
q.e: Graphite, a form of carbon used as pencil lead, conducts electricity — the odd one out among non-metals.

q.t: Why do cooking pans have wooden or plastic handles?
o: Wood and plastic are poor conductors of heat
q.e: The metal pan conducts heat into the food; the handle is a poor conductor, so it stays cool enough to hold.

q.t: Magnesium oxide dissolved in water turns red litmus blue. So magnesium oxide is…
q.e: Red → blue means a base. Metal oxides are basic.

q.t: Sulfur dioxide dissolved in water turns blue litmus red. So it is…
q.e: Blue → red means an acid. Non-metal oxides are acidic.

q.t: What colour flame does magnesium ribbon burn with?
q.e: Magnesium burns with a dazzling white flame and leaves white magnesium oxide powder.

q.t: Plastic, glass and wood are…
q.e: 'Metal' and 'non-metal' sort elements. Plastic, glass and wood are not elements, so they are neither.

q.t: The green coating on old copper and black coating on silver are examples of…
q.e: Corrosion is the slow eating away of a metal surface by air, water or other substances. Rusting is corrosion of iron.

q.t: Guitar strings are made of metal because metals are…
q.e: Metals can be drawn into thin, strong wires — they are ductile.

q.t: In the rusting experiment, why is silica gel put in bottle A?
o: To remove moisture from the air
q.e: Silica gel dries the air, so bottle A has air but no water. The nail there does not rust.

q.t: Why is the water in bottle B boiled and covered with oil?
o: To remove air and keep it out
q.e: Boiling drives out dissolved air; the oil layer stops air getting back in. So bottle B has water but no air.

q.t: Only bottle C (air + water) rusted. What does this prove?
o: Both air and water are needed
q.e: Each other bottle removed one ingredient and didn't rust. So rusting needs both together.

q.t: How does painting an iron gate prevent rusting?
o: It keeps air and water off the iron
q.e: Rust needs air and water to touch iron. Paint forms a barrier between them.

q.t: An element X is burned and its oxide turns blue litmus red. X is most likely a…
q.e: An acidic oxide comes from a non-metal.

q.t: An element Y is shiny, rings when struck and its oxide is basic. Y is a…
q.e: Lustre, sonority and a basic oxide are all signs of a metal.

q.t: Wood does not flatten and does not shatter when hammered. Which is correct?
o: Wood is neither malleable nor brittle
q.e: Not being malleable doesn't automatically mean brittle. Wood does neither.

q.t: Why do electricians wear rubber gloves and shoes?
o: Rubber is a poor conductor of electricity
q.e: Current can't easily pass through rubber, so it protects the electrician.

q.t: 1 gram of gold can be drawn into a wire about how long?
q.e: Gold is so ductile that a single gram makes a wire around 2 km long.

q.t: Sulfur burns in air to form a gas. In water this gas forms…
q.e: Sulfur dioxide dissolves in water to make sulfurous acid — a non-metal oxide giving an acid.

q.t: Sodium is kept in kerosene but phosphorus in water. What do both choices have in common?
o: Each keeps the substance away from what it reacts with
q.e: Sodium reacts with air and water, so kerosene shields it. Phosphorus reacts with air, so water shields it.

q.t: A bridge near the sea rusts faster than one in a desert. The best reason:
q.e: Rusting needs air and water. The moist sea air supplies plenty of water.

q.t: Mercury is a metal but liquid. Sodium is a metal but soft. What do these tell us?
o: Not every metal has every typical property
q.e: They are exceptions — useful reminders that the usual metal properties have exceptions.

q.t: You have two unlabelled grey powders. Burning each and testing the oxide in water with litmus: P's oxide turns red litmus blue. P is…
q.e: A basic oxide (red → blue) comes from a metal.

q.t: Why is the Iron Pillar of Delhi famous?
o: It has barely rusted for over 1600 years
q.e: Despite standing in the open for centuries it shows very little rust — evidence of advanced ancient Indian metal-working.

q.t: Which property would you use to tell a metal spoon from a plastic one in the dark, using only sound?
q.e: Strike them: the metal rings, the plastic gives a dull sound.

q.t: Why does a nail kept in oil not rust?
o: Oil keeps air and water off the iron
q.e: Like paint and grease, oil covers the surface so air and water can't reach the iron.

q.t: Which pair is matched WRONGLY?
q.e: Coal is a non-metal and brittle, not malleable.

q.t: How many elements are known so far?
q.e: Scientists have found 118 elements — substances that can't be broken into simpler ones.

q.t: Rain in an area with factories burning sulfur-rich coal is acidic. Why?
o: Sulfur dioxide dissolves in rain to form an acid
q.e: Burning sulfur gives sulfur dioxide, a non-metal oxide. In water it forms an acid, making the rain acidic.
